content: A cystocele, also known as a prolapsed bladder, is a medical condition that occurs when the wall between a woman’s bladder and her vagina weakens. This weakening allows the bladder to droop or bulge into the vagina. This condition can lead to discomfort and issues with emptying the bladder completely. Cystoceles often develop due to muscle strain, which may occur during childbirth, heavy lifting, or repeated straining during bowel movements. The hormone estrogen plays a role in maintaining the strength of the muscles around the vagina. Therefore, cystoceles are more common after menopause, as estrogen levels decrease. When the bladder drops from its normal position, it can cause two primary problems: involuntary urine leakage and incomplete bladder emptying. In some cases, the fallen bladder stretches the opening of the urethra, leading to urine leakage during activities that increase pressure on the bladder, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or physical movement. Cystoceles are classified into three grades based on severity. A mild cystocele (grade 1) occurs when the bladder droops only slightly into the vagina. A more severe cystocele (grade 2) occurs when the bladder sinks far enough to reach the vaginal opening. The most advanced form (grade 3) occurs when the bladder bulges out through the vaginal opening. A doctor can often diagnose a grade 2 or grade 3 cystocele based on the patient’s symptoms and a physical examination of the vagina, as the fallen part of the bladder is usually visible. A diagnostic test called a voiding cystourethrogram may also be used. This test involves taking X-rays of the bladder during urination to assess its shape and identify any issues that may obstruct the normal flow of urine. Additional tests may be required to evaluate other parts of the urinary system. Treatment options for a cystocele depend on its severity. For mild cases, no treatment may be necessary, and the doctor may simply recommend avoiding heavy lifting or straining to prevent the condition from worsening. For moderately bothersome symptoms, a pessary may be recommended. A pessary is a device inserted into the vagina to support the bladder and keep it in place. Pessaries come in various shapes and sizes to ensure a comfortable fit for the patient. However, they must be removed regularly to prevent infections or ulcers. In cases of large or severe cystoceles, surgery may be required to reposition the bladder and secure it in a more normal position. This procedure is typically performed by a gynecologist, urologist, or urogynecologist. Patients undergoing this surgery should expect to stay in the hospital for several days and allow 4 to 6 weeks for full recovery.
